title: Mistakes at work

cards: The report has already gone out to the whole team, and the totals at the bottom are wrong. Nobody has noticed yet. There's a small window, about the length of a coffee, when the mistake belongs only to its maker.
It could be fixed quietly. It could be left to see if anyone spots it. Or there's a hard message to send, just three words long: that was me.
Old texts from two very different places speak to that window. Today: Zigong.

teach.b: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy."
Two moves after the mistake: confess it, say it out loud; forsake it, stop doing it. What doesn't prosper isn't the mistake. It's the covering.

teach.h: THE REAL FAULT IS NOT CHANGING.
teach.b: In the Analects he says, more or less: to have a fault and not change it, that is what's really called a fault. The first slip is ordinary; hands slip. The real fault, for Confucius, comes after, in the refusal to change.
Third, his student Zigong adds a picture.
A noble person's faults, he says, are like eclipses of the sun and moon. When he errs, everyone sees it. When he changes, everyone looks up to him.
An eclipse doesn't hide. It happens in full view, it passes, and the light comes back where everyone can see it. Fourth, putting it to work.
Own it, fix it, learn: the phrase is modern, but the old texts hold each step. Confess is owning it. Forsake is fixing it and not repeating it.
Change is learning. At work, it fits in two plain sentences.
I got that wrong. Here's what I'm doing about it. No speech, no long account of why it wasn't really your fault.
Just the eclipse, in full view, and then the light.

how: Readers of the Analects return to its sayings on faults as a guide to self-correction, and Jews and Christians read Proverbs 28:13 as a call to confess wrongs and turn from them.

o: the sage who wrote down the book of Proverbs
Confucius's student who likened faults to eclipses
a Chinese word for saving face after a slip

games.q: what's inside a mistake owned — tap the pairs.

s: Proverbs promises mercy to the one who covers a mistake well
he that covereth his sins shall not prosper; mercy goes to whoso confesseth and forsaketh them.
in the Analects, Zigong compares a noble person's faults to eclipses
everyone sees them, and when he changes, everyone looks up to him.
Confucius says the true fault is making a mistake at all
the true fault is having one and not changing it.

games.q: you're the noble person in Zigong's saying, and you've made a mistake everyone can see. what does he say happens when you change?
games.why: like an eclipse: everyone sees the fault, and when it passes, everyone looks up.

practice: Bring to mind one recent mistake, at work or at home, nothing dramatic, and notice the urge to explain it, soften it, make it smaller, then let that pass by.
Silently try the plain sentence, I got that wrong, and name one small fix and one thing you'd do differently next time.
If someone should hear it, let their face come to mind; if you pray, you can bring the mistake to God in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Zigong. Confucius's student who said a noble person's faults are like eclipses: seen by all, then lit again when changed. Today's word.

orig.say: GWAW er boo GAI, shr way GWAW yee
orig.note: Chinese, Analects 15.29: to err and not change, this is called a fault. 過 (guò) is the word for a fault.

carryVoice: Your line: own it. A fault in full view passes, like an eclipse. Day nine hundred twenty, done.
